extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, critics, and students of the craft of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting narrative method and point of view for novels: when to use pictorial/omniscient narration versus scenic/dramatic presentation, how to prepare climaxes, create character, and manage economy and repetition across a sustained story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture as preparation for drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s picture, as preparation for his drama — an opening descriptive picture lays up the reserve of effect needed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a rich, methodical opening picture (architecture, portraits, furniture, garden, etc.) that can be gradually denuded to register the protagonist’s ruin or change; Balzac’s method: amass descriptive resources early so the later destruction/decay can be shown with renewed force rather than lost by repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of the climax (reserve effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; it should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loading the climax with material that could be dispatched earlier; prepare and 'lay up' the climax in earlier pages so the final touch is small but decisive. Don’t betray preparatory artwork by calling attention to it — preparation should be unrecognizable until it attains its end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sudden, implausible climactic strokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst kind of disappointment does not happen like that, falling as a stroke; it steals into a life and spreads imperceptibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story’s psychological truth is gradual, avoid hinging the climactic effect on a single sudden discovery or contrived incident; prefer slow, cumulative diminution (the 'slow chill' in Eugénie Grandet) that fits human experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain a single effect by increasing repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The book must remain throughout reiterating one effect with growing intensity—always at the pitch of high hope and sharp disappointment, always prepared to heighten and sharpen it a little further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narratives about a fixed idea or obsession, structure repeated outbreaks or failures so each recurrence increases intensity rather than diminishing force; use external signs (loss of possessions, social standing) to renew the effect visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a tangible world you can destroy
rubrics_metrics.description: He has created so much that there is plenty to destroy; only at last ... is the wreck complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate setting and social world with concrete, valuable things (house, portraits, silver, garden) early on so progressive loss has visible, cumulative impact on reader’s perception of ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety of preparation (do not betray the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of preparation is no art if it betrays itself at the outset, calling attention to its purpose. By definition it is unrecognizable until it attains its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make anticipatory details feel natural and incidental rather than deliberately telegraphing the climax; the reader should perceive the completed stroke, not the machinery that led to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject dictate the method
rubrics_metrics.description: How far he may choose to push the process in his book—that is a matter to be decided by the subject; the subject dictates the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between scenic/dramatic presentation and pictorial/retrospective narration based on what the theme requires (study of a consciousness, panoramic scope, or immediate action). Do not force a congenial method onto a subject it cannot serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic (scenic) method: limit and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic story is strictly scenic; it allows no such freedom as exposition and retrospect; it is limited to so much as the ear can hear and the eye see. In rigid drama there is naturally no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic form when the story can be expressed through visible action and dialogue. Be aware of the sacrifices: inner thought and panoramic survey are excluded and must be transmuted into action to be dramatized effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (narrative/omniscient) method: retrospective fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pictorial book the narrator must gather up his experience, compose a vision of it as it exists in his mind, and lay that before the reader; it is the reflection of an experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retrospective narration or an omniscient viewpoint to present broad, time-spanning impressions and to explore inner life and background that cannot be rendered scenically. The natural mode is recall, meditation, and summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed method — enter consciousness selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy’s mixed method: scene is laid to scene and, within the scene, he is ready to enter the consciousness of any or all the characters at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing scenic action with interior focalization can render crowded casts vivid, but it must be managed carefully; inconsistency or insufficient preparation (as with Anna Karenina’s early crisis) can make key actions feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient preparatory condensation for immediate crises
rubrics_metrics.description: If the situation is to be really made and constituted, the space it may cover must be tightly packed; the method should be that which most condenses and concentrates the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a narrative forces a character into a high-stakes crisis early, condense and concentrate the background (use pictorial summary or focused exposition) so the reader can gauge the stakes and the character’s motives without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show inner mind in the moment rather than only by report
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story involves a searching exploration of his own consciousness, an account in his own words, after the fact, is not by any means the best imaginable. Far better it would be to see him while his mind is actually at work in the agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For psychological realism, prefer present-tense or immediate-in-scene techniques of focalization (showing thought as it occurs) over retrospective summaries, which can feel second‑hand and less convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as dramatized spokesman to gain authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If the spell is weakened... introduce another point of view, to set up a fresh narrator to bear the brunt of the reader’s scrutiny. The author is dramatized; his 'assertions gain in weight' when supported by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a distinct narrator-character to lend credibility and to shift responsibility for assertions away from an omniscient authorial voice; this dramatizes the telling and can make the narrative self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch the timing of character exposure vs plot demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Anna must be represented upon such a critical height of emotion before there is time... to create the right effect for her and to make her impulse really intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance how early and how fully a character is rendered with when the plot requires them to act. Premature exposure to high drama without adequate inward rendering can make passions feel unearned or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, vivid scenes to enrich character and speed story
rubrics_metrics.description: A passing glimpse... in half a page he makes an unforgettable scene. The half-page is not a diversion or an interlude; it speeds the story by augmenting the tone and the value of the lives that we are watching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ short, sharply observed moments to add texture and depth to characters. These micro-scenes accumulate to create fuller personhood and can propel the narrative by enriching the reader’s emotional investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of dramatization for large or inner-focused subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic form is out of the question... wherever the main burden of the story lies within some particular consciousness, the growth of a character, or where the story is too big or too comprehensive to be treated scenically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing a purely dramatic (scene-only) method onto subjects that require panoramic survey, extended reflection, or intimate psychological study; choose pictorial or mixed methods where necessary.
